verification.method: Independent syllabus authoring, explicit biological marking points and displayed-data calculation checks

parts.prompt: Calculate the net carbon sequestration during the year.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State whether this modelled system is a net carbon sink or source and justify your answer.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the result cannot guarantee permanent carbon storage.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State one uncertainty that should be included in a more complete budget.

steps.text: 8 tonnes of carbon.
A sink, because removal exceeds release over the stated period.
Stored carbon can later be released by decomposition, disturbance or fire / changing environmental conditions.
Accept one: measurement uncertainty, methane emissions, exported dissolved carbon, imported organic matter or year-to-year variation.

title: Seasonal timing divergence 1
stem:
The table shows constructed mean dates in two decades, expressed as day of year. The caterpillar peak is a major food resource for great-tit chicks.

|Event|Earlier decade|Later decade|
|---|---|---|
|Peak caterpillar abundance|135|124|
|Peak chick food demand|136|132|

steps.text: Earlier: 1 day; later: 8 days; both needed.
The separation increases, so peak food demand occurs further after peak caterpillar abundance.
Less food may be available when chicks need it most, reducing growth / survival and hence parental reproductive success.
Food-peak width, alternative food, variation between years and actual chick survival / breeding output are not shown.

title: Arctic plant growth and reindeer arrival
stem:
The table shows constructed mean dates in two decades, expressed as day of year. The spring growth of Arctic mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium arcticum) is a food resource for arriving migratory reindeer (Rangifer tarandus).

|Event|Earlier decade|Later decade|
|---|---|---|
|Peak nutrient-rich chickweed growth|142|128|
|Peak reindeer arrival|143|137|
